news.title: Katie Zakaria, who worked with Trump in the elections, will become the new White House press secretary
news.text:
Conservative political commentator Katie Zakaria has been offered the position of White House press secretary. Donald Trump called her a "loyal associate" and a "dedicated participant in the MAGA movement," writes the BBC.

"She previously participated in my election campaigns, helping to work in key 'swing' states where we won," Trump wrote on Truth Social.

"I am confident that as White House press secretary, Katie will achieve significant results for the benefit of our country, as she is respected by media representatives and the American people, and will be able to establish excellent cooperation with both the press and U.S. citizens, as well as with my administration."

Zakaria thanked Trump on the social network X: "To serve President Trump and the American people at this crucial historical moment — as the country celebrates its 250th anniversary — is the greatest honor for me."

Zakaria, who currently works as a communications advisor for Trump Media & Technology Group, will be the sixth official representative of the president during his two administrations.

She previously held the position of press secretary for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for a short period.

Former White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt, who left her position in August, is reportedly moving to Fox News this week.

42-year-old Katie Zakaria frequently appears on conservative TV channels Newsmax and Fox News and actively participates in the political activities of the Republican Party. Specifically, in 2006, when George W. Bush was the US President, she interned at the Republican National Committee and the White House Office of Political Affairs.

According to her LinkedIn profile, she has served as Senior Communications Advisor for Trump's media company and on the Truth Social platform since June. She worked at the Department of Homeland Security for a very short period—from February to March of this year.

Zakaria has long and actively defended President Trump and his administration's policies.

In a June interview with the BBC, she disputed criticism of Trump regarding the UFC mixed martial arts tournament fight held at the White House, stating that UFC principles are "the very principles upon which our constitutional republic was founded."

"It's about not stopping the fight until the very end," she said. "I think there's no better embodiment of the American spirit than a good UFC fight."

news.title: Trump's AI rebrand is catching on with Elon Musk and Marc Benioff
news.text: Donald Trump wants two letters scrubbed from the tech industry’s vocabulary, and some executives are already reaching for replacements. Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff said Friday that his company’s AIForce platform is getting a new name. “The era of Super Intelligence is here. AIForce is officially SIForce,” Benioff wrote on X. The announcement follows Elon Musk’s pledge Sunday to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, giving Trump’s campaign to replace “artificial intelligence” with “super intelligence” traction beyond Washington. Salesforce’s change concerns its agent platform, rather than the company’s corporate name. Trump, meanwhile, is turning his terminology preference into a test. “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” Trump wrote on Truth Social on Thursday. The warning escalates a push Trump formalized in a September 29 executive order directing federal agencies to substitute “Super Intelligence” and “SI” for “Artificial Intelligence” and “AI” in official communications, websites, reports, and policy documents, to the extent permitted by law. Private companies aren’t required by the order to follow suit. But Benioff’s announcement and Musk’s proposed rebrand show how the president’s preferred language is making its way into corporate branding. The administration’s argument is that AI has outgrown its name. The executive order says today’s systems increasingly amplify human creativity and that “Super Intelligence” better captures their potential. The rebranding push complicates matters for companies whose names include AI, and raises questions over what counts as superintelligence. The term generally describes systems far more capable than humans across a broad range of tasks, and renaming existing products doesn’t establish that they meet that threshold. OpenAI, Scale AI, Character AI, and Resolve AI did not respond to requests for comment.
news.summary: Trump wants "AI" replaced with "Super Intelligence." Marc Benioff and Elon Musk have already pledged corporate rebrands.

 Market Bag: Sorrel scarce, lettuce reaches $2,000 







KINGSTON, Jamaica — Jamaicans may have to dig deeper into their pockets for one of Christmas’ most beloved staples, as vendors at the Coronation Market warn that sorrel could be both scarce and expensive this year.

The festive favourite, traditionally used to make the popular Christmas drink, would normally be making its way into the market by now. However, sorrel was nowhere in sight when Market Bag visited this week, raising concerns about its availability ahead of the holiday season.

With drought conditions continuing to affect agricultural production, vendors say shoppers could face higher prices this year.

“You might search the whole market and you don’t find it. If you do find it, it’s still gonna have a price,” one vendor warned. “Anytime things get scarce, the less it is, the more the price goes up so I won’t put a fixed price because I’m not sure as yet. But the point still remains: if you pay $1,500 last year, now we have the drought, it would be maybe about $2,000.”

Meanwhile, prices for other produce remain high at Coronation Market this week, with lettuce climbing to as much as $2,000 per pound and plantains selling for $3,000 per dozen. Ripe bananas were going for $1,000 per dozen, while tomatoes were priced at $500 per pound.

Sweet peppers were selling for $400 per pound and Scotch bonnet peppers for $600 per pound. Onions and Irish potatoes dipped to $250 per pound, while sweet potatoes increased slightly to $450 per pound.

news.title: Trump Slams Nobel Peace Prize Winner as ‘Mystery Person’ in New York Rally
news.text: President Donald Trump took aim at this year’s Nobel Peace Prize winner during a rally in Syracuse, New York, on Friday, calling the recipient a “mystery person,” saying he should have won instead. “Today they gave out the Nobel Peace Prize to a person I never heard of. Nobody did. It's a mystery person,” Trump said, adding that the decision was “an indelible stain” on the country of Norway, which hosts the Nobel committee. South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay won the Nobel Peace Prize for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The Norwegian Nobel Committee praised her commitment to justice and human dignity as “a source of hope and inspiration to all who seek to bring about a more peaceful world.” Trump again talked about how he has ended multiple wars and conflicts, saying he had “settled eight wars” and was about to “settle or win two more,” referring to Iran and the Russia-Ukraine war. Trump rallied supporters at Syracuse’s Oncenter in support of Republican gubernatorial candidate Bruce Blakeman, who is seeking to unseat Democratic Governor Kathy Hochul. Local reports described the venue as packed. Boxing legend Mike Tyson also joined Trump at the rally, while hundreds of protesters gathered outside. Trump Takes Swipes at NY Leaders After Bronx ICE Shooting Trump’s visit comes a day after a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE)-involved shooting in the Bronx’s Marble Hill neighborhood sparked protests and prompted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Hochul to call for a halt to enforcement operations. Trump addressed the incident during his remarks Friday night, slamming New York’s sanctuary policies—saying they are designed to protect criminals. “Just yesterday, our heroes of ICE apprehended a man with a criminal record a mile long who was wanted for possible murder, and murder in a gang,” Trump said. “He’s a very dangerous man and they got him. But instead of being praised, ICE was scorned by New York politicians who set him loose, they want to set him loose.” On Friday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin ruled out a halt to immigration enforcement. “We’re not putting a pause on enforcement,” he told reporters. “I'm sorry, we're not. In fact, I'm not sorry.” Oscar Belgal, 28, was shot Thursday afternoon during what authorities described as a “targeted enforcement operation.” The Department of Homeland Security told Newsweek that Belgal is a Dominican national who is in the U.S. illegally and has a prior conviction for grand larceny. The department also cited prior arrests in which he was accused of assault, robbery, drug possession and weapons possession, as well as alleged associations with the Trinitarios gang. A judge has since temporarily blocked his deportation while the court reviews his legal challenge. Hochul said she had spoken with the mother of the 5-year-old boy who was in the car at the time of the shooting. “Last night, I spoke with the mother of the five-year-old boy who was in the backseat when ICE agents opened fire on his father’s car,” Hochul wrote on X. "Thank God she isn’t planning a funeral for her little boy today." She said Trump confirmed that ICE would not return to the family, following their phone call Thursday. Videos Show Protesters Escorted Out of New York Rally Three protesters heckled Trump during his nearly 90-minute speech and were escorted out. “You know they're all paid protesters, right?” Trump said. Moments later, another protester began shouting as the crowd chanted “USA” and booed. Trump said, “His mother just called him, ‘Get out of there, son.’” As he has at several recent rallies, Trump urged the Syracuse crowd to “pretend” he’s on the ballot. “Please pretend I’m on the fricking ballot,” Trump told the crowd, urging supporters to rally behind Republicans ahead of the midterm elections, just 25 days away. Blakeman is seeking to become New York’s first Republican governor in 20 years. George Pataki, who left office in 2006, was the state’s last GOP governor. A Harvard CAPS/Harris poll conducted on September 26 found that 42 percent of voters had not firmly settled on their midterm choice. Grant Davis Reeher, professor of political science at Syracuse University, told Newsweek that the number of undecided voters could potentially benefit Republicans. “Especially in those close Senate races that Republicans have won more easily in the past,” he said. “Those folks might ‘come home’ in the final week of the election.” Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Anna Commander and Edward T. Cummins

news.title: Trump blasts Nobel Peace Prize decision as ‘indelible stain’
news.text:
Washington: US President Donald Trump has sharply criticised the Nobel Peace Prize committee for overlooking his claims of having ended eight international conflicts, calling the decision an embarrassment and a disservice to the United States.

Addressing a Republican election rally in Syracuse, New York, Friday, Trump said his administration had achieved an unprecedented record in resolving international disputes and argued that the United States deserved recognition for those efforts.

“The United States of America, represented by me as your President, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn’t,” Trump told supporters.

He described the decision as “an indelible stain” and accused the Norwegian Nobel Committee of allowing political considerations to influence its selection.

Trump said he had helped resolve eight conflicts and was working towards agreements involving Russia, Ukraine and Iran.

“I settled eight wars,” he declared, arguing that each of the conflicts he claimed to have resolved could have justified a separate peace prize.

Beyond South Asia, Trump listed disputes involving Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, Armenia and Azerbaijan, Egypt and Ethiopia, and Israel and Hamas among the conflicts he claimed to have resolved.

He also credited himself with preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and averting wider regional warfare.

Trump said his administration was now moving towards resolving the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the confrontation with Iran.

“Russia, Ukraine we’re going to get that all done, too, and that’s happening quickly,” he said.

He also issued a warning to Tehran, saying that Iran would have to meet American demands or face further consequences.

The President criticised the Nobel committee’s decision to recognise another recipient, saying he was unfamiliar with the person selected for the 2026 award.

He accused the committee of failing to acknowledge what he described as extraordinary American diplomatic achievements.

Trump also expressed frustration with the United Nations, claiming that the organisation had played no meaningful role in the conflicts he said his administration had resolved.

“In all of the wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations they were of no help to me,” he said.

The President argued that the award should have recognised the United States rather than an individual, saying his administration’s peace efforts were undertaken on behalf of the American people.

His criticism came during a campaign rally supporting Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 congressional elections, where he also highlighted his administration’s economic, immigration and national security policies.

The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded by the Norwegian Nobel Committee, an independent five-member body appointed by Norway’s parliament. The prize recognises individuals and organisations considered to have made significant contributions to peace, international cooperation and conflict resolution.

news.title: Trump Cornered On Kimberly Guilfoyle’s Wild Demand for Secret Cash
news.text:
President Donald Trump has responded to a string of explosive allegations about Kimberly Guilfoyle, the U.S. ambassador to Greece and his eldest son’s former fiancée. 

Guilfoyle allegedly asked a MAGA donor Eric Deters to pay off her $100,000 American Express bill in exchange for access to Trumpworld figures, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday. She is also facing a State Department inspector general probe into allegations involving improper gifts, private travel, and other conduct.

Guilfoyle’s lavish lifestyle has also made headlines, as has her closeness to a Greek lobbyist.

While leaving the White House for a rally in Syracuse, New York, Trump was asked by a reporter about the mounting allegations against Guilfoyle.

“I just heard about it. It’s too bad,” Trump replied, without elaborating on what, exactly, he found regrettable.

“I mean, I don’t know. She’s—she’s an ambassador,” he continued. “I just heard a little bit about it. I don’t know too much, but she was always very nice.”

Guilfoyle, 57, was engaged to Donald Trump Jr., 48, from late 2020 to 2024. She was previously married to Trump foe Gavin Newsom from 2001 to 2006. 

A former Fox News host, Guilfoyle left the network in July 2018, reportedly after being given an ultimatum to resign or be fired amid a sexual harassment accusation by a colleague. (Guilfoyle has denied the claims.) 

After exiting Fox, she worked for a pro-Trump super PAC, then on Trump’s 2020 presidential campaign. In 2024, she spoke at the Republican National Convention—one of her final public appearances with Donald Trump Jr.

According to the Journal report, Guilfoyle wanted Deters to pay off the American Express bill before her confirmation hearing last July. She also wanted the transaction handled off the books.

“It won’t show up anywhere if you wire money to American Express,” she texted Deters over Signal, according to the Journal. “Please.”

In another message, Guilfoyle allegedly wrote: “Honey please I need you to get this done for me today. You could just send it here.”

Deters never paid the $100,000, saying doing so would harm his marriage. The former Kentucky congressional candidate was reportedly seeking Guilfoyle’s help in “getting the attention of the new Trump administration on some personal tax and legal issues,” according to the report.

Deters wrote that, over the years, he had paid Guilfoyle $300,000, but had “not received one favor.”

Guilfoyle’s lawyer, Jesse Binnall, told the Journal that his client disputes the messages’ authenticity, but did not specify which messages she challenged. Binnall claimed Guilfoyle “was owed a balance for traveling to and supporting these patriotic events.” Deters claims he didn’t owe Guilfoyle anything.

A U.S. Embassy spokesperson responded to the report by saying, “Guilfoyle’s career in and out of public service is guided by deep and abiding values. The bipartisan Senate Foreign Relations Committee fully vetted her, and the U.S. Senate confirmed her. The Ambassador remains committed to representing the American people with dedication and integrity.”

Democrats on the House Oversight Committee have asked Guilfoyle to provide documents related to the allegations, which some say have raised questions about a possible pay-for-play arrangement. 

California Rep. Robert Garcia said Deters’ claim that Guilfoyle had acted this way with other right-wing donors was troubling.

“This alleged misconduct raises serious public corruption and national security concerns,” Garcia wrote to Guilfoyle in a letter. “If Trump Administration officials can be bought by donors, the American people suffer the consequences of corrupt leaders more concerned with their own enrichment than the public good and vulnerable to blackmail by foreign intelligence services.”

Deters himself told MS NOW that Guilfoyle’s $100,000 request “absolutely was a quid pro quo.”

Meanwhile, the State Department probe into Guilfoyle comes amid reports that she demanded complimentary high-end champagne and a nearly $1,800 meal at a five-star restaurant along the Athens Riviera, the Daily Mail reported.

The same outlet also described two incidents that paint a less flattering picture than Trump’s description of Guilfoyle as “very nice.”

Guilfoyle allegedly demoted two of her drivers because she did not like the way they “made a left turn,” the Mail reported. She also reportedly demoted the top agent on her security detail because he didn’t answer her 4 a.m. call to deliver ice cubes while she was drinking.

Guilfoyle has also faced scrutiny over her connection with Christos Marafatsos, a 39-year-old lobbyist for Greek infrastructure and energy group Aktor. 

Marafatsos has attended meetings with foreign officials where Guilfoyle has promoted Aktor, but he did not disclose that he works for the company, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The White House did not immediately respond to the Daily Beast’s request for comment.

Guilfoyle allegedly asked a MAGA donor Eric Deters to pay off her $100,000 American Express bill in exchange for access to Trumpworld figures, The Wall Street Journal reported Wednesday.  ‘Stew Peas’ up for six awards at Saturday’s Caribbean Film Awards 







The cast and production team of Jamaican psychological thriller Stew Peas are gearing up for Saturday’s inaugural Caribbean Film Awards, where the locally produced film will be vying for honours in six categories.

Among those in contention is popular Jamaican entertainer Kerry-Ann “Chiney K” Collins, who earned a Best Actress nomination for her role in the film.

The production, written, directed and produced by Sosiessia Nixon-Kelly, is also nominated for best feature film, best director, best screenplay, Caribbean Heritage Film Award and Caribbean Film of the Year.

With the awards ceremony just a day away, the nominations have once again placed the spotlight on the Jamaican thriller, which has been making strides both locally and internationally.

The recognition comes ahead of the film’s regional theatrical release on October 29, when it is scheduled to open in seven Caribbean territories through Caribbean Cinemas.

The rollout will include Trinidad and Tobago, Barbados, Antigua, Guyana, St Lucia, St Kitts and the US Virgin Islands, ahead of a limited United States theatrical release in January 2027.

According to production company iKon Media & Films, Stew Peas will become the first Jamaican film distributed by Caribbean Cinemas, marking a significant milestone for the local film industry.

The thriller follows Detective Tessa Riley as she investigates the murder of her best friend, unaware that a mysterious housekeeper is secretly working to destroy her marriage.

Drawing on Jamaican folklore and West African spiritual traditions, the film stars Collins alongside Tarique Barrett, Shernet Swearine and Quera South. It was filmed entirely in Kingston.

Following its premiere at Carib 5 in Kingston on June 27, the film opened in cinemas across Jamaica on July 22 and has maintained a presence on local screens.

Speaking recently about the film’s growing regional reach, Nixon-Kelly welcomed the support for Caribbean productions.

“Every new territory confirms what we’ve known all along: Caribbean audiences are hungry for authentic, homegrown cinema, told in our own voice on the big screen,” she said.

The six nominations now present another opportunity for Stew Peas to gain regional recognition as the Jamaican production awaits Saturday’s awards ceremony.

news.title: Russian presidential aide says Putin-Trump conversation was substantive, friendly
news.text:
Details of phone call

Russian and US officials began preparing for the call on October 7, when Ushakov spoke by phone with US Special Presidential Envoy Steve Witkoff. Witkoff conveyed Trump’s birthday wishes to Putin.

"Steve Witkoff also said that Trump wanted to congratulate Putin personally by phone. We then began looking for a convenient time for the call, taking into account the time difference between Moscow and Washington. We also had to consider Putin’s planned departure for the CIS summit in Turkmenistan on the morning of October 8.

"We eventually agreed that the best option would be to speak as soon as our president returned from that trip."

"President Trump postponed some events that had been scheduled for today, and so the phone call took place late in the evening on October 9."

Putin and Trump had a "very substantive," even friendly conversation that lasted an hour and a half.

"Donald Trump immediately warmly congratulated Vladimir Putin on his birthday and wished him success and well-being. He also remembered to convey greetings from his wife, Melania," Ushakov said.

"Nobody wanted to hang up first. In light of that, I hope the US president will not be offended if I quote his words that he was ‘ready to continue communicating with Vladimir Putin today, this evening, tonight and the next day.’"

Putin and Trump expressed satisfaction with the communication channels functioning between the two countries through their presidential administrations, intelligence services and other relevant agencies.

"As for the substance of the conversation, I, of course, cannot satisfy your curiosity, dear colleagues. I also cannot go into detail about the specific issues the presidents discussed."

Kiev’s actions and the situation on the battlefield

Putin told Trump that Russia’s position on the goals and objectives of its special military operation remains unchanged. Russia also remains ready for a political and diplomatic settlement to achieve a lasting and sustainable peace.

Ushakov said the possibility of resuming trilateral talks involving the United States and Ukraine had been discussed during the presidents’ previous conversation, with negotiations potentially restarting immediately after Russia’s State Duma elections. "The situation is different now," he said.

Kiev’s attempts to disrupt parliamentary elections in Russia had effectively undermined the possibility of immediately resuming negotiations. "And now, as the president said, we will consider when these negotiations can be resumed," Ushakov added.

Putin also spoke in detail about Russia’s response to Ukrainian attacks.

"Vladimir Putin spoke in detail about the measures we are taking in response to terrorist attacks by the Kiev regime, which has opted for escalation and every possible means of prolonging the conflict," Ushakov said.

Putin told Trump that Russian forces have full control of the initiative along the line of contact and are advancing confidently.

"It was emphasized that Kiev’s attempts to halt the advance of Russian forces along the entire line of contact by launching strikes deep into our territory have no chance of success. Our armed forces have full control of the initiative and are advancing confidently," Ushakov said.

Prospects for an in-person meeting

Putin said he values the attention the US leadership is devoting to dialogue with Russia despite its domestic agenda and involvement in Middle Eastern affairs.

The presidents did not discuss specific dates for their next in-person meeting.

Putin and Trump currently plan to attend the APEC summit in China and may find an opportunity to meet there.

"An important international event is coming up in China - the APEC summit. At least for now, both the Russian and US leaders are interested in attending. Accordingly, if both leaders are at the same international venue, I assume they will find an opportunity to meet, shake hands and talk," Ushakov said.

Economic initiatives and petroleum products

"The two leaders discussed preparations for major economic initiatives in detail, including potential supplies of Russian petroleum products to US and global markets. The Russian and US presidents have already issued a special statement on the matter," Ushakov said.

Humanitarian cooperation

Putin thanked US First Lady Melania Trump for her contribution to reuniting children with their families in Russia and Ukraine.

Regarding concerns about the humanitarian situation in Alyoshki, in the Kherson Region, it was agreed that Russian Human Rights Commissioner Yana Lantratova would remain in regular contact with Melania Trump’s staff.

The situation surrounding Iran

"Vladimir Putin specifically emphasized that diplomatic options on the Iran track have by no means been exhausted: an agreement with Tehran can and should be reached through negotiations," Ushakov said.

Putin also told Trump that Moscow’s offer to transfer Iran’s enriched uranium to Russia remains on the table.

Witkoff hopes to meet Putin soon

"Steve Witkoff asked me to add his own and Jared Kushner’s (a US businessman and Trump’s son-in-law - TASS) warmest wishes to our president, whom he sincerely respects and hopes to meet soon," Ushakov said.

news.title: 'Weak decision by strong partners': Zelensky bashes Trump's oil deal with Russia
news.text: Digital Desk | Kyiv, Oct 10 (IANS) Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has strongly criticised US President Donald Trump's agreement allowing Russia to supply diesel to the United States and global markets, arguing that the move would provide Moscow with additional funds to sustain its war against Ukraine and undermine ongoing efforts to secure peace. In a lengthy post on social media platform X, Zelensky said that allowing Russia to generate revenue through petroleum product exports would strengthen the Kremlin's ability to continue military operations rather than encourage an end to the conflict. "Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilised world," Zelensky wrote. "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged," he added. Trump on Friday (local time) announced a major agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin under which Moscow would supply millions of tonnes of diesel to the United States and global markets, saying the move would bring down fuel prices sharply. The announcement came at a time when a Ukrainian negotiating delegation was in Florida for two days of discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner. The talks focused on possible arrangements to end the war, including a proposal for a ceasefire that would halt attacks on energy infrastructure. In a post published on Truth Social on Friday afternoon, Trump described his conversation with Putin as highly successful and outlined the proposed scale of Russian diesel supplies to international markets. "I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter," Trump wrote. The US Treasury Department also issued a temporary licence that eases sanctions on Russian diesel exports, facilitating the proposed supply arrangement. Zelensky questioned the timing of Trump's announcement, particularly because the Ukrainian delegation was engaged in discussions with American officials on possible ways to bring the conflict to an end. He suggested that the Ukrainian team's presence in Florida could be serving as a "smokescreen" for the agreement reached between Washington and Moscow. Speaking to reporters, the Ukrainian President stressed that his country's representatives were in the United States to discuss ways to stop the fighting and secure a ceasefire, making the announcement of the Russian diesel deal particularly concerning for Kyiv. He then pointed to the contrast between the ongoing negotiations involving Ukrainian and American officials and the simultaneous communication between Trump and Putin, whom he described as "the leader of this war". Zelensky argued that the revenue Russia would earn from diesel exports could directly contribute to sustaining its military campaign and prolonging the suffering caused by the conflict. "Means more money for this war, more money to inflict suffering on us, without a doubt," he said, referring to the financial benefits Moscow could obtain from the agreement. "It only feeds Putin and gives him the ability to fight even more," Zelensky said, describing the agreement as a "weak decision by strong partners".

news.title: Trump attacks Nobel Peace Prize decision
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 10 (IANS) US President Donald Trump has sharply criticised the Nobel Peace Prize committee for overlooking his claims of having ended eight international conflicts, calling the decision an embarrassment and a disservice to the United States. Addressing a Republican election rally in Syracuse, New York, on Friday, Trump said his administration had achieved an unprecedented record in resolving international disputes and argued that the United States deserved recognition for those efforts. "The United States of America, represented by me as your President, should have received the Nobel Peace Prize, but didn't," Trump told supporters. He described the decision as "an indelible stain" and accused the Norwegian Nobel Committee of allowing political considerations to influence its selection. Trump said he had helped resolve eight conflicts and was working towards agreements involving Russia, Ukraine and Iran. "I settled eight wars," he declared, arguing that each of the conflicts he claimed to have resolved could have justified a separate peace prize. Beyond South Asia, Trump listed disputes involving Kosovo and Serbia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Rwanda, Armenia and Azerbaijan, Egypt and Ethiopia, and Israel and Hamas among the conflicts he claimed to have resolved. He also credited himself with preventing Iran from acquiring nuclear weapons and averting wider regional warfare. Trump said his administration was now moving towards resolving the Russia-Ukraine conflict and the confrontation with Iran. "Russia, Ukraine we're going to get that all done, too and that's happening quickly," he said. He also issued a warning to Tehran, saying that Iran would have to meet American demands or face further consequences. The President criticised the Nobel committee's decision to recognise another recipient, saying he was unfamiliar with the person selected for the 2026 award. He accused the committee of failing to acknowledge what he described as extraordinary American diplomatic achievements. Trump also expressed frustration with the United Nations, claiming that the organisation had played no meaningful role in the conflicts he said his administration had resolved. "In all of the wars that I have settled, I never spoke to the United Nations they were of no help to me," he said. The President argued that the award should have recognised the United States rather than an individual, saying his administration's peace efforts were undertaken on behalf of the American people. His criticism came during a campaign rally supporting Republican candidates ahead of the November 3 congressional elections, where he also highlighted his administration's economic, immigration and national security policies. The Nobel Peace Prize is awarded by the Norwegian Nobel Committee, an independent five-member body appointed by Norway's parliament. The prize recognises individuals and organisations considered to have made significant contributions to peace, international cooperation and conflict resolution.

news.title: Trump Names Truth Social Adviser Katie Zacharia as New White House Press Secretary
news.text:
US President Donald Trump announced Friday, Oct. 9, that he had selected Katie Zacharia, a senior communications adviser at the company behind his Truth Social platform, as the new White House press secretary, replacing Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down in August.

Trump confirmed the appointment in a post on Truth Social, praising Zacharia’s loyalty and experience in political communications.

A California native, Zacharia previously served as a spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security and worked on Trump’s presidential campaigns, including efforts targeting battleground states.

She currently serves as a senior communications adviser at Trump Media & Technology Group, which operates Truth Social, the platform Trump frequently uses to announce major government decisions.

In announcing her selection, Trump credited Zacharia with helping his campaigns in the seven swing states he won in the 2024 presidential election.

He described her as a loyal supporter from the beginning and expressed confidence that she would succeed in her new position.

Trump also said Zacharia was respected by journalists and would work effectively with the media, the American public and his administration.

From Truth Social to the White House

Zacharia, an attorney and conservative political commentator, has appeared on Fox News and Newsmax and previously held communications roles in Republican politics.

She joined Trump Media & Technology Group in June 2026, following a brief stint at the Department of Homeland Security.

According to her professional background, she began her political career as an intern with the Republican National Committee during President George W. Bush’s administration.

Zacharia holds undergraduate and law degrees from Pepperdine University and previously worked as general counsel for the conservative organization Fix California.

Zacharia will succeed Karoline Leavitt, who left the position in late August.

news.title: Trump Says Russia To Supply Diesel To US, Zelenskyy Calls It 'Gift To Putin'
news.text:
US President Donald Trump on Friday announced a deal under which Russia will supply diesel to American and global markets, hailing the arrangement as a way to bring down fuel prices ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, however, has criticised the move, calling it a “gift to Putin” and warning that easing sanctions without a lasting de-escalation agreement could help Moscow prolong its war against Ukraine.
Trump said that Russian President Vladimir Putin had agreed to immediately supply more than 300,000 metric tonnes of diesel, equivalent to around 2.25 million barrels of fuel. The US administration has also temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian fuel, restrictions originally intended to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war in Ukraine.
Speaking to reporters outside the White House before travelling to Syracuse, New York, for a midterm election campaign event, Trump described the arrangement as a major development for the US fuel market.
“I think you heard about the oil deal with Russia. That is a big deal. That is massive amounts of oil coming into our country. I want to thank President Putin. We have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it is diesel, which is what we want,” Trump said.
The announcement comes as diesel prices remain near record levels, putting pressure on farmers, ranchers, truckers and other consumers who depend on the fuel. Prices fell following the announcement, although analysts cautioned that the proposed supplies might not be sufficient to keep them down.
The development also carries political implications for Trump's Republican Party ahead of the November 3 congressional elections, which will determine whether it retains its narrow control of Congress.
Trump Announces Further Russian Diesel Supplies
In a post on Truth Social, Trump outlined plans for additional Russian diesel shipments beyond the initial supply of more than 300,000 metric tonnes.
He said Russia would provide another 500,000 tonnes during November, followed by one million tonnes immediately thereafter and a further three million tonnes within a short period, depending on the condition of Russian diesel refineries.
Trump argued that the Russian supplies, alongside what he described as US control of the Strait of Hormuz, would help reduce diesel prices in America and elsewhere.
“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” he wrote.

He identified lowering fuel costs for Americans, particularly farmers, ranchers and truckers, as his “Greatest Priority”. Trump also reiterated that Iran would not be permitted to possess a nuclear weapon.
After the announcement, Kirill Dmitriev, an envoy for Putin, praised US-Russia cooperation in a post on X. Dmitriev had asked US officials during a visit to Washington last month to grant licences allowing all major Russian oil companies to export diesel to the American market, Reuters reported, citing sources familiar with the matter.
Russia's Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak had recently said that the country's diesel market was balanced. According to Russian state news agency TASS, Novak said Moscow would consider partially reopening exports if domestic production exceeded demand.
Zelenskyy Says Easing Sanctions Would Help Russia Continue War
Zelenskyy criticised the proposed arrangement, arguing that relaxing restrictions on Moscow without a clear and lasting agreement to reduce hostilities would undermine efforts to end the conflict.
In a post on X, the Ukrainian president called for stronger sanctions against Russia, continued military and other support for Ukraine, and greater pressure on Moscow to stop the war.
“Peace never comes through weakness. Today, representatives of the U.S. Congress were in Kyiv – a bipartisan delegation – and I am grateful to them for visiting Ukraine at such a difficult time. They asked: what is needed to end the war? The answer must be strong. There must be sanctions under the Lindsey Graham bill, there must be support for Ukraine in protecting lives, and there must be pressure on Russia for its war,” he wrote.
Zelenskyy argued that easing sanctions without a durable agreement would allow Russia to continue its military campaign and cause further damage.
“Any easing of sanctions against Russia without a clear and lasting de-escalation agreement with Russia is an obvious weakness. It plays into Russia’s hands – allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.
Referring specifically to the proposed diesel supplies, Zelenskyy described the arrangement as a concession that could benefit Moscow rather than advance peace.
“Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world. Russia will ‘repay’ the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged,” he said.
In a phone interview with Axios on Friday, Zelenskyy also described Trump's decision to ease sanctions and allow Russian diesel exports as “not fair and not honest”.

Ukraine Offers Reciprocal Steps To De-Escalate Conflict
Zelenskyy also outlined a proposal under which Ukraine would stop striking Russian oil refineries if Moscow ceased attacks on Ukraine's energy infrastructure.
“Ukraine will not set Russian oil refineries on fire if Russia does not destroy our energy infrastructure. This is the kind of agreement we are proposing to America, and we believe the United States has enough power to achieve such a compromise,” he said.
The Ukrainian president's remarks came as Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner met Ukraine's negotiating team in Miami. According to Axios, senior diplomats from Germany, France, the United Kingdom, the European Union and NATO were also involved in discussions on new US proposals aimed at ending the war.
The competing positions highlight the tension between Washington's stated aim of bringing down fuel prices and Kyiv's demand that economic pressure on Moscow remain in place until there is a meaningful agreement to de-escalate the conflict.

news.title: Putin tells Trump peace talks are unlikely, cites Ukraine drone attacks  | Barbados Gazette – Barbados &
news.text:
Russian President Vladimir Putin has said an immediate resumption of peace talks with Ukraine is unlikely, citing drone attacks on Moscow during parliamentary elections last month.

In a phone call with US President Donald Trump on Friday, Putin said Moscow was ready to resume negotiations with Kyiv after the parliamentary elections. However, the drone attacks on the capital made the resumption of trilateral peace talks between Russia, Ukraine and the US unlikely.

“By launching a large-scale drone attack on Moscow, other cities and polling stations on the most important day of the elections, and by targeting some people involved in organising the elections, the Kyiv regime has, in reality, interrupted the possibility of an immediate resumption of the negotiation process,” said Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov about the call with Trump.

“As the president said, we will now assess when these negotiations can resume,” he added regarding the trilateral talks.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Thursday that Russia’s war in Ukraine is at a dangerous stalemate and the United States will keep working towards a deal to end the war.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said earlier this week that the country was ready to hold trilateral talks with the United States and Russia this month.

Earlier on Friday, Donald Trump announced after the call with Putin that Russia agreed to deliver more than 300,000 tonnes of diesel to American and global markets.

The deal was criticised by US lawmakers, Zelenskyy and European allies.

Zelenskyy called the agreement a “gift to Putin”.

“All that money goes toward the war against people, against Ukraine, against all of us. I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair,” he said in a statement.

In response to the US-Russia diesel deal, a government spokesperson said the United Kingdom would continue to “maintain pressure on Russia through the toughest sanctions regime ever imposed by the UK.”

news.title: Isaias makes landfall along the US Gulf Coast as a dangerous Category 2 hurricane
news.text: GULF BREEZE, Florida — Hurricane Isaias crashed into the US Gulf Coast as a dangerous Category 2 storm on Friday, lashing communities with wind and rain and threatening to flood low-lying areas where residents were advised to evacuate ahead of its arrival.The first hurricane of the Atlantic season made landfall near Destin, Florida, the Miami-based National Hurricane Center said. It had maximum sustained winds of 105 mph (169 kph). The storm weakened to just below major hurricane status before it came ashore.High winds whipped palm trees and thundering waves crashed along the beaches of the Florida Panhandle and Alabama on Friday as Isaias approached.“The storm is here. Buckle down at this point. Don’t be getting out on the roads,' Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said at a news conference, adding that flash flooding would be a hazard 'throughout the region.”Forecasters warned of a significant storm surge, damaging winds, flooding and possibly even tornadoes before the storm loses steam as it moves inland and delivers strong winds and rain well north into Atlanta.Hurricane-force winds lashed the Gulf shoreline in the low-lying coastal area known for powdery white sand beaches that are dotted with vacation homes, waterfront bars and seafood shacks.In Mobile, Alabama, officials reported downed trees and power lines, while Emerald Coast Utilities Authority, which serves parts of Florida, issued a boil-water notice for its customers.More than 400,000 customers in Florida and Alabama were without power Friday evening, according to poweroutage.com.A hurricane warning was in place from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to the western Florida Panhandle. Several counties announced mandatory evacuations while Mobile, Alabama, imposed a curfew beginning Friday evening until morning.Residents in Panama City, Florida, braved the rain while filling sandbags Friday to protect their houses.“I mean, it’s just the nature of the beast. It’s Florida,' said Corliss Stone, who works for the fire department.Many will brave Isaias at homeOne of the biggest concerns is a storm surge that could be as high as 6 to 9 feet (1.8 to 2.7 meters), according to the hurricane center. Places most at risk include Florida’s Pensacola Beach and the Gulf Islands National Seashore.Anne Petzold, who lives with her husband in the Florida beach community of Gulf Breeze, said everyone in their neighborhood planned to ride out the storm. The couple installed hurricane shutters and picked up anything in their yard that could turn into a projectile.“Everybody does what they can do, everybody asks if they need help — they ask for help, they offer help. All good,” she said. “It’s just another adventure.”Dangerous conditions are expected throughout the western panhandle, southern Alabama and southern Mississippi, the National Hurricane Center said.In a sign of how serious the warnings are, dozens of Waffle Houses in the Florida Panhandle were closed, according to the company's website. The beloved Southern breakfast chain is known for staying open through severe weather and often is a measuring stick of a storm’s severity.Kelsei Frazier, a Florida-native living in Pace who is no stranger to hurricanes, knows all about the Waffle House Index.“We joke because if Waffle House is still open, then you know it’s not a bad hurricane, but all the Waffle Houses that I know of within at least a normal range from us are closed,” said Frazier. “Which is a pretty big deal.”Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis warned residents to expect power outages, gasoline shortages and closures of bridges and highways.The state's National Guard deployed about 5,000 soldiers and airmen to help with the response, and search and rescue teams were ready to respond, while some prisons evacuated inmates.The whole region could get soakedIsaias is expected to weaken and be downgraded to a tropical storm by Saturday afternoon, the center said.Still, heavy rain is forecast as it moves inland, with 4 to 8 inches (10 to 20 centimeters) or even more expected through the weekend from southern Alabama to southwestern Georgia.Isaias, which is the first hurricane to hit the eastern U.S. since Milton tore up the Gulf Coast of Florida in 2024, also is expected to bring heavy rain and potential flooding to much of the Southeast over the weekend, and then to parts of the Midwest and Northeast into Monday.Isaias grounds flights but likely to miss oil hubsThe storm grounded most Friday flights at several Panhandle airports, including all flights into and out of Destin-Fort Walton Beach Airport. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, scrapped his plans to attend Saturday’s football game between the University of Georgia and the University of Alabama in Tuscaloosa. He said he didn’t want to disrupt the emergency response.Isaias was expected to miss the oil industry’s biggest hubs along the Gulf Coast, but fuel prices could rise if power outages shut down refineries for processing crude, industry experts said.On Dauphin Island, a barrier island off the Alabama coast, Mayor Jeff Collier said he didn't expect major damage, “but at the same time, these things are very fickle and a little jog here or there, or some last-minute increase in strength — we just have to be prepared for the worst.”Meanwhile in the Pacific, Hurricane Simon became a Category 2 storm on Friday and was expected to strengthen further before making landfall in Mexico this weekend.Tropical Storm Rachel was also expected to bring heavy winds and rain to northern Mexico and Southern California over the weekend.

news.title: Anthropic cites new AI misbehavior, some on government sites
news.text: Anthropic said its Claude AI model carried out additional unintended actions on the digital systems of outside organizations, including some U.S. government agencies’ websites, prompting a warning from U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration for artificial intelligence companies to secure their systems.In a report outlining previously undisclosed incidents, Anthropic listed four types of unintended behaviors that the AI has demonstrated, including exploiting basic flaws in software to run commands, submitting forms it should not have and bypassing restrictions to access certain public data.The company said that some of the cases involved websites run by government agencies at the federal, state and local levels, without specifying the agencies. news.title: Ex-US Ambassador: Trump’s Russian Diesel Deal Won’t Lower Prices but Will Undermine Peace
news.text:
Former US Ambassador to Ukraine Steven Pifer condemned President Donald Trump’s decision to lift sanctions on Russian diesel as “very unwise,” warning in an exclusive interview with Kyiv Post on Friday, Oct. 9, that the move would help finance Moscow’s war machine while undermining Washington’s own efforts to negotiate peace.

Pifer, who served as US ambassador to Ukraine from 1998 to 2000, said the agreement would send American money directly into Russia’s economy, enabling the Kremlin to purchase more weapons for its continuing attacks on Ukraine.

“This is a very unwise decision,” Pifer told Kyiv Post.

“First of all, it means that American dollars will be going to purchase Russian fuel, and that’s going to help the Russian military machine buy more missiles and bombs to use against Ukraine.”

The former ambassador argued that Trump’s decision was particularly damaging because Washington was supposed to be increasing pressure on Moscow to negotiate an end to its invasion, not offering the Kremlin economic relief.

“Second of all, it completely undercuts Trump’s own effort to mediate a solution to the Russia-Ukraine war, at a time when the US should be putting more pressure on Moscow to negotiate seriously,” Pifer said.

“In fact, he’s relieving that pressure, because this will make it harder to achieve peace between Russia and Ukraine.”

Little relief for US fuel prices

Pifer, now a nonresident senior fellow at the Brookings Institution and an affiliate of Stanford University’s Center for International Security and Cooperation, also challenged the economic rationale for Trump’s agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, arguing that the initial diesel shipments were too small to significantly affect US fuel prices.

“If you look at the amount of diesel fuel that he hopes to buy – 300,000 tons in October – that amounts to less than one half a day’s consumption of diesel fuel in the United States,” he said.

“That’s not going to have that big an impact on the price of diesel.”

Trump announced Friday that Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel to US and global markets, followed by another 500,000 tons in November, 1 million tons afterward and an additional 3 million tons depending on the condition of Russian refineries.

The administration subsequently issued a temporary authorization allowing certain transactions involving Russian diesel, reversing restrictions intended to deprive Moscow of energy revenues.

The White House has presented the agreement as a way to ease soaring diesel prices for American farmers, truck drivers and consumers.

However, energy analysts have questioned whether the additional supplies will produce lasting price reductions, given the scale of American demand and global refining constraints.

Pifer expressed hope that the administration might reverse course.

“It’s a very unfortunate decision. I hope that there’s a chance that it will be reconsidered,” he said.

Will Republicans challenge Trump over Graham sanctions?

The former ambassador also questioned how Republican lawmakers would respond to Trump’s decision after Congress passed legislation designed to increase economic pressure on countries purchasing Russian energy.

“It will be interesting [to see] the Republicans, who had passed the Graham sanctions bill, which was to apply greater sanctions on countries that buy Russian energy – how they’re going to react when Mr. Trump now says the United States will be buying Russian energy,” Pifer said.

Trump’s agreement came just three weeks after he signed the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act into law on Sept. 18.

The legislation was intended to expand economic pressure on Russia’s energy sector and financial networks supporting its invasion.

The new diesel arrangement has raised questions about the administration’s willingness to enforce those restrictions even as Ukraine continues pressing Washington to cut off Moscow’s war revenues.

‘No evident movement by the Russian side’

Asked about the prospects for the latest US-led peace negotiations, Pifer expressed deep skepticism.

The talks were taking place in Florida, where US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner were meeting Ukrainian and European officials to explore possible ways to end Russia’s full-scale invasion.

One proposal under consideration involved a partial ceasefire covering energy infrastructure.

But Pifer expressed little hope for progress, citing Russia’s unwillingness to compromise.

“I have not had much expectation that these talks would produce anything, because while Ukraine, I believe, has shown a readiness to make some painful decisions to try to find a compromise to end the war, there has been no evident movement by the Russian side,” he told Kyiv Post.

He pointed to previous statements by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov as evidence that Moscow had not softened its negotiating demands.

“The Kremlin spokesman, Dmitry Peskov, said six weeks ago that Russia’s position had not changed from the one announced by Vladimir Putin in December 2024,” the former US envoy said.

“And that suggests that Mr. Witkoff and Mr. Kushner have failed to get the Russians to move on any significant issue.”

The former ambassador said he saw little reason for optimism about the current diplomatic process.

“So I do not have many hopes for this negotiation process at this point.”

Pifer warned that Trump’s decision to ease sanctions would only reinforce Moscow’s resistance to compromise.

“This decision makes it even harder, because Moscow sees the US easing pressure rather than pushing the Kremlin to negotiate seriously,” he said.

President Zelensky also sharply criticized Washington’s decision, saying Ukraine’s negotiating team in Florida was being used as a “smokescreen” while Trump reached a separate energy agreement with Putin.

“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen,” Zelensky said Friday.

“And that is definitely unfair. And it is a weak decision by strong partners.”
news.summary: In an exclusive Kyiv Post interview, former US Ambassador to Ukraine Steven Pifer called Trump’s decision to ease Russian diesel sanctions “very unwise,” warning it would help finance Moscow’s war, undermine peace negotiations and have little impact on US fuel prices.

news.title: Chris Rock Makes an Excellent Point About Wokeness
news.text:
I have to confess that I have a huge crush on Chris Rock. 

That said, I really wasn't even a fan of his until I saw his Selective Outrage Netflix special a few years ago. It came about at a time in my life when I needed some laughs, and I felt it delivered. I've since gone back and watched most of his body of work from over the decades, including his Saturday Night Live appearances, most of his movies, his old talk show, his older stand-up specials, and even a lot of past interviews. 

For what it's worth, he's matured beautifully through the years, and I love how he isn't trying to impress anyone these days, or so it seems. He calls things as he sees them. And while I doubt he and I would see eye-to-eye on all things politics, he's the kind of Democrat I don't mind having a conversation with because he comes across as fairly honest and isn't afraid of criticizing his own side of the aisle or admitting when it's defeated. He also sees people as people... not elephants and donkeys. 

That's exactly what he did last week in an interview with David Marchese of The New York Times. Rock has a new movie, which actually comes out today — Friday, October 9 — called Misty Green. He wrote, directed, and starred in it, and the previews look excellent. He's also been making the media rounds, promoting it. During this particular interview, he described exactly what's wrong with wokeness today. 

"The problem with quote, unquote, wokeness — and don’t get me wrong, it is great that marginalized people have a voice; it is great to advocate for anybody that feels marginalized," Rock began, admitting that he's not against the concept in general. "But the problem is we’re in the Old Testament right now, and the Old Testament has no forgiveness. The Old Testament didn’t work, so they had to write a remix called the New Testament." 

I didn't quite understand the biblical analogy — either that or he's not getting the relationship between the Old and New Testaments wrong — but I fully understood what he said next: "The problem is when you institutionalize it." 

He used the Salem Witch Trials as an example. 

"The Salem witch hunts. I’m sure the first three witches they caught were actually f***ing witches," he said. "But then you open up a witch office and now you’ve got to start lying. Now you’ve gotta f***ing make s*** up because you’ve got overhead. You’ve got to justify the witch hunters’ f***ing pensions."

His point is that this country didn't just go woke in recent years. We went woke and then turned it into bureaucracy. And now we have to create more targets to keep those offices open and fully staffed. 

Again, Rock said he's glad some of it happened because some deserving people did get some good things out of it, but he basically suggested that this should have happened from ordinary accountability, not permanent enforcement. 

He likened it to faith and friendship. The comedian said he has a friend who he wasn't going to name who "might have gotten canceled." He said people ask him all the time why he's still friends with that person. His response to that? "If you’re only friends with your friends when they’re good, they’re not your friends." He also reminded us that God forgives. 

Again, Rock is a liberal Democrat who doesn't like Donald Trump and does see some value in efforts we, on this side of the aisle, might consider woke. But he's not afraid to admit that his side took it, institutionalized it, and made it so that it runs on outrage. 

If we must share the country with leftists, I'll take more like him. 

I'll leave you with the trailer for Misty Green. I hope to check it out soon.

Each ⁠year of his presidency, Trump ‌has expressed disappointment ‌at his failure to ​win the prize.

“This ‌is an indelible stain on ‌the country of Norway and those people that made such a disgraceful and embarrassing decision,” Trump said.

He listed a number of ‌conflicts that he claimed a role in resolving and said he ⁠has ⁠helped prevent wars from breaking out between North and South Korea, Japan and North Korea, and China and Taiwan, without providing evidence.

“The Nobel Peace Prize has been forever discredited by a handful of radical ideologues who are anti-democracy and really enemies of civilization. And we will not ​forget, Norway,” he said.

 Key processes remain incomplete for implementation of demerit system—Vaz 







KINGSTON, Jamaica—Transport Minister Daryl Vaz says although the demerit points provisions under the Road Traffic Act and its regulations are in force, the Island Traffic Authority’s (ITA) administrative and business processes remain incomplete to facilitate the assignment of points and the suspension or revocation of licences following court decisions.

The minister said discrepancies in the data from the traffic management system across the Jamaica Constabulary Force (JCF), the judiciary, and the ITA, coupled with the backlog of traffic tickets awaiting adjudication, continue to impede full implementation.

The Transport Authority in August had announced a delay in the October 1 implementation of the demerit point system until a full revision is completed. The revision is expected to incorporate recommendations from the committee, as well as the rollout of an education programme.

“The agreed delay will allow for the completion of the required processes, correction of data, inconsistencies and determination of the necessary legislative remedy to reset existing demerit points, ensuring at all times that there is fairness, equitableness, transparency, collaboration and effective implementation of the system,” Vaz said.

The minister reiterated that there will be a zero-tolerance approach for traffic violators once the implementation of the system is complete.

 Trump appoints ‘devoted fan’ Katie Zacharia as press secretary 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP)—United States (US) President Donald Trump on Friday announced the appointment of conservative commentator Katie Zacharia as his new White House press secretary, praising her as a loyal supporter.

“She has an unblemished record of support, and has been a loyal and brilliant supporter, right from the beginning,” Trump posted on his Truth Social platform.

“She is, likewise, a devoted fan and member of MAGA!” he added, referring to his Make America Great Again movement.

Zacharia, a lawyer and communications adviser to Trump’s media company, will succeed Karoline Leavitt, who stepped down in August after becoming one of the most prominent public faces of his second administration.

Trump hailed his new spokeswoman’s credentials, including her work for his presidential campaigns, and said he was confident she would enjoy a good relationship with the White House press corps.

“I am confident that Katie will deliver strong results for our Country as the next White House Press Secretary,” he said.

An administration official had earlier confirmed to AFP that Zacharia had been offered the high-profile position, following initial reports of her selection in US media.

Zacharia currently serves as a senior communications advisor to Trump Media and Technology Group, which operates the president’s Truth Social platform.

Trump described her work at his company as “outstanding.”

A frequent commentator on conservative television networks including Fox News and Newsmax, Zacharia previously served a brief stint as a spokeswoman for the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees US immigration enforcement.

– High profile role –

She joined the department under then-secretary Kristi Noem earlier this year but left after around two months, according to her LinkedIn profile.

Zacharia, who lives in California, has also worked with Fix California, a conservative advocacy group founded by Richard Grenell, a longtime Trump ally and one of his special presidential envoys.

According to CNBC, she serves as general counsel for the organization, which seeks to advance conservative political causes in the Democratic-leaning state.

A graduate of Pepperdine University’s law school, Zacharia began her career in Republican politics, working as an intern for the Republican National Committee in 2006, CNN reported.

Trump sought advice from several allies and advisors, including Leavitt, before deciding to offer Zacharia the position, according to CNN.

Her appointment fills one of the White House’s most visible positions, with the press secretary responsible for briefing journalists, fielding questions about administration policies and serving as a chief public defender of the president.

Leavitt, who took up the position when Trump returned to power in January 2025, became the youngest White House press secretary in US history at 27.

A staunch Trump loyalist who previously served as press secretary for his 2024 presidential campaign, she left the administration in late August following the birth of her second child.

Fox News announced this week that Leavitt would join the conservative network as an on-air contributor beginning in November.

Trump praised his outgoing spokeswoman, saying she had done a “fantastic job” in the role.

news.title: Mike Tyson Makes Baffling Trump Prediction
news.text:
Former heavyweight boxing champion Mike Tyson made a bold prediction about the midterms, declaring that Donald Trump will win. 

There’s just one problem: the president isn’t on any ballot

Tyson made the baffling comment while speaking to reporters in the White House briefing room Friday before accompanying Trump to a political rally in Syracuse, New York. 

When a reporter asked Tyson, who was smiling, what he and the president had talked about, he responded “golly,” and dodged the seemingly simple question. He then appeared to turn to White House aides, saying: “I can’t believe you guys put me up here.” A White House staffer piped up: “No tough questions.” 

Asked whether Republicans would win the midterms, the former boxing champion replied: “I think Donald Trump’s gonna win.” He offered no further explanation.

As Trump, 80, and Tyson, 60, walked to Marine One en route to Syracuse, the president quipped to reporters: “I won’t be fighting him today... We’ve been friends for a long time. Iron Mike: There’s nobody like him.” Tyson fought a number of his matches at Trump casinos in Atlantic City.

Trump has made a habit of cozying up to sports figures, particularly fighters. His enthusiasm for combat sports culminated in a UFC cage match outside the White House to celebrate the nation’s 250th anniversary and his own 80th birthday. Trump’s own athletic pursuits, meanwhile, are largely limited to golf.

He has played on 140 known days out of 628 days in his second term as of Friday, or about 22.3 percent of his presidency, according to Trump Golf Track.

Tyson last appeared at a Trump-related political function last month, when he attended the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) summit in Washington. He was also featured in a Super Bowl ad blasting processed food and encouraging Americans to eat “real food.”

The unlikely duo’s friendship has endured decades of controversy, including Trump’s outspoken defense of Tyson following his 1992 rape conviction.

Tyson was convicted of raping 18-year-old beauty-pageant contestant Desiree Washington in his Indianapolis hotel room and was sentenced to six years in prison. He served nearly three years. Trump, at the time, told shock jock Howard Stern that Tyson’s conviction was a “travesty,” and that it was women who “start grabbing” Tyson when he walks into a room.

“I’ve seen women going around touching him,” Trump said. “He walks in a room and the women start grabbing him and grabbing his a-- and grabbing anything else they can grab on him.”

Trump also told New York Magazine that Tyson had told him the teenager “wanted it real bad.”

Tyson made the baffling comment while speaking to reporters in the White House briefing room Friday before accompanying Trump to a political rally in Syracuse, New York. 

Read more at The Daily Beast.

news.title: Energy minister Chris Bowen rules out using Russian fuel as Middle East fuel crisis continues
news.text:
Climate Change and Energy Minister Chris Bowen has ruled out dipping into Russian fuel supplies as the conflict in the Middle East continues.

Addressing the media on Saturday, Mr Bowen was asked for his views on a fuel trade agreement between Russia and the United States.

President Donald Trump this week revealed he had come to an arrangement for Russia to supply the US with 1.8 million tonnes of diesel as prices soar amid the conflict with Iran.

But Mr Bowen emphatically ruled out following suit.

“We don’t need or want Russian fuel in Australia,” he said.

“We have arrangements in place as best we possibly can with our trading partners to ensure that Russian fuel does not flow in Australia.”

Ruling out a similar trade agreement, Mr Bowen took personal aim at the Russian president.

“We do not want Vladimir Putin to benefit from this war in the Middle East,” he said.

“What the United States does is a matter for them, but we won’t be changing our approach.

“We continue to have a very, very firm view that Russia should not be rewarded for their illegal and immoral invasion of Ukraine by any arrangements put in place.

“We have our policy and it is very clear.”

Meanwhile, with diesel prices having recently eclipsed the $2 mark once again as the US-Iran conflict rumbles on, Mr Bowen confirmed the status of Australian fuel supplies in the face of supply disruption.

“Australia has 43 days worth of petrol, which is two days more than my update last week,” he said.

“We have 31 days worth of diesel, one day less than last week, and we have 30 days of jet fuel.

“We have 51 ships on the way to Australia with fuel and we have 3.2bn litres of various fuel locked in and scheduled to be delivered over the next four weeks.”

He said the continued supply should give Aussies “reassurance” over availability at the bowsers.

“We are working very closely with trading partners in South-East Asia and beyond and with our domestic refiners to ensure they are working at full pelt and in the longer term building Australia’s sovereign capabilities.”
news.summary: Energy Minister Chris Bowen has revealed whether Australia could dip into Russian fuel supplies after the US announced its new trade deal.
news.author: David Hannant

news.title: Trump envoys discuss ‘winter preparedness’ with Kiev and its European NATO backers
news.text:
US President Donald Trump’s top envoys have begun two days of negotiations with Ukrainian and European representatives in Miami, focusing on preparations for the coming winter and potential ways to de-escalate the Ukraine conflict on terms that would be acceptable to Moscow.

Special Envoy Steve Witkoff described Friday’s discussions as “constructive,” saying US representatives had discussed prospects for a “lasting peace” with Kiev and its most hawkish European backers, including Britain, France and Germany, as well as officials from the European Commission and NATO.

The talks covered “near-term measures related to winter preparedness,” including energy resilience and grain exports, as well as longer-term security guarantees, post-war reconstruction and Ukraine’s potential accession to the EU, according to Witkoff.

“The exchange was productive and helped identify areas for further exploration ahead of the United States’ next engagement with Russia,” he wrote on X.

The negotiations were scheduled to continue on Saturday, and no concrete agreements or breakthroughs have been announced so far.

The US delegation is led by Witkoff and Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, while Kiev is represented by Vladimir Zelensky’s chief of staff, Kirill Budanov, foreign intelligence chief Rustem Umerov, deputy chief of staff Sergey Kislitsa and senior lawmaker David Arakhamia.

The European delegation includes Bjoern Seibert, chief of staff to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, and national security advisers from Britain, France and Germany. NATO is represented by Geoffrey van Leeuwen, chief of staff to Secretary General Mark Rutte, according to European media reports.

The talks follow reports that Witkoff and Kushner were preparing to present “new ideas and proposals” aimed at breaking the diplomatic deadlock. According to Axios, the pair could travel to Moscow later this month for further talks with Putin.

One proposal under consideration reportedly involves a partial ceasefire covering strikes on energy infrastructure, amid growing anxiety among Kiev’s European backers over the economic and energy consequences of the conflict.

“They are all nervous about the winter. It will be a tough winter if the war does not stop,” a US source previously told AFP.

The Miami meeting also coincided with a 90-minute phone conversation between Trump and Putin on Friday, during which the leaders discussed Ukraine, Iran and a major agreement to resume Russian diesel supplies to American and global markets.

Zelensky lashed out at Trump, effectively accusing Washington of stabbing Kiev in the back by striking a separate diesel deal with Moscow. Zelensky branded the move “a weak decision by strong partners” and accused the US of using the Ukrainian delegation in Miami as a “smokescreen” while negotiating with Putin behind Kiev’s back.

Trump has repeatedly pressed Zelensky to halt Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil refineries, blaming them for worsening a global diesel shortage and driving up fuel prices for American consumers. According to Kremlin aide Yury Ushakov, Trump promised Putin that he would convey Moscow’s position to the Ukrainian delegation in Miami.
news.summary:
The Miami talks focused on near-term issues like “energy resilience” ahead of Washington’s next round of negotiations with Moscow

news.title: Vance backs Ramaswamy in Ohio governor race
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 10 (IANS) US Vice President JD Vance has thrown his weight behind Indian-American entrepreneur Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for Ohio governor, portraying him as a businessman capable of creating jobs, lowering energy costs and providing property tax relief as Republicans step up their campaign ahead of the November 3 midterm elections. Addressing a Republican rally in Lima, Ohio, Vance praised Ramaswamy's business background and said his experience would help revive manufacturing, attract investment and improve economic opportunities in the state. "Vivek is an entrepreneur. He's a guy who hasn't just received a paycheck he signed a paycheck to," Vance told supporters, drawing a contrast between the Republican candidate and career politicians. The Vice President, who previously represented Ohio in the US Senate, said Ramaswamy understood the challenges facing businesses and working families. "What Vivek is gonna do is he's gonna to attract jobs and he's gonna unleash the incredible potential of this state," Vance said. He said Ramaswamy would focus on reducing living costs, particularly energy expenses, and creating conditions for businesses to expand their operations in Ohio. Vance also highlighted Ramaswamy's proposal to provide property tax relief to homeowners, presenting it as a central element of the Republican candidate's economic agenda. "He's gonna get historic property tax relief for every single citizen who owns a house in this state," he said. The Vice President described Ramaswamy as someone capable of translating policy proposals into action. "Vivek is not like so many politicians, a person who just talks about things," Vance said, adding that the candidate had demonstrated an ability to execute his ideas. Ramaswamy, a biotechnology entrepreneur and former Republican presidential candidate, is seeking the governorship against Democrat Amy Acton. Vance sharply criticised Acton over her role in Ohio's response to the COVID-19 pandemic, accusing her of supporting restrictions that disrupted schools, religious gatherings and family activities. His criticism was part of a broader attack on Democrats, whom he accused of pursuing policies that increased costs and weakened American manufacturing. The Vice President also campaigned for Republican Senator Jon Husted, who is seeking election to the Senate seat previously held by Vance. He credited Husted with supporting the Trump administration's tax and economic policies, including measures affecting overtime income, tips and Social Security benefits. Vance argued that Republican leadership was essential to maintaining what he described as an economic revival in Ohio. He pointed to manufacturing investments involving automobile, aerospace and pharmaceutical companies, claiming that administration policies were encouraging businesses to expand domestic production. "We've created 72,000 manufacturing jobs just in 2026 alone," Vance said. The employment figure was presented as an administration claim and was not independently verified in the speech. Vance also defended President Donald Trump's tariff policies, arguing that companies investing in American manufacturing should receive tax incentives while businesses moving jobs overseas should face financial penalties. "But if you're sending American jobs overseas, if you're trying to ship your factory to a foreign corporation or you're trying to replace American workers with a legal immigrant later, you know what you're gonna get? A big fat tariff," he said. The Vice President's remarks reflected the administration's emphasis on domestic manufacturing, immigration restrictions and economic nationalism as Republicans campaign to retain political control in Washington. Vance also attacked former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, who is challenging Husted, accusing him of supporting policies that harmed American workers and encouraged illegal immigration. He urged Republican supporters to turn out in large numbers on November 3, describing the elections as critical to continuing the Trump administration's economic agenda.
