news.title: Trump Announces Russian Diesel Deal as US Eases Fuel Sanctions
news.text: WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections. Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia will deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time” after that, he wrote. Trump’s shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia’s energy revenues, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called it, “a weak decision, unfortunately, a weak decision by strong partners," according to a statement released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington. Trump’s announced the deal as his envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner were meeting with Ukrainian officials to discuss a proposal to try to end the Russia-Ukraine war. “I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelenskyy said. Trump's move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas. Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia’s war but said, “Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority.” Washington and Moscow offer few details on deal The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3. Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. While diesel futures prices dipped on Friday’s news, the national average price per gallon of diesel in the U.S. was still $6.23, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22. A statement from Putin, released by the Kremlin on Friday, said that during their call he and Trump dedicated “significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis” and also discussed “the situation around Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations.” Russia “confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets,” Putin said. “I am confident that this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy.” The two leaders agreed to continue contacts, Putin said in the statement. Trump and Putin's deal draws immediate backlash Zelenskyy, in a lengthy post online reacting to the deal, said Russia would repay it “with further terror and perfidy.” He cast it as an investment in the war, allowing it to be prolonged. “It plays into Russia’s hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said. Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump’s announcement “infuriating.” “This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn’t the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia,” Beyer said in a statement on X. “Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he’s lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels.” The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt. It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports. The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because of Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. news.title: Kamala Harris's husband opposes another White House bid: Report
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Oct 10 (IANS) Former US Vice President Kamala Harris is considering another presidential run in 2028, but her husband, Doug Emhoff, has privately expressed reservations about the prospect, while some Democratic donors have warned that another campaign would face significant challenges, according to a media report. The Wall Street Journal reported on Friday that Emhoff has told people privately he would prefer Harris not to seek the presidency again, although those close to him expect he would support her if she decides to enter the race. The report, citing people familiar with the conversations, said Harris has been taking steps that could lay the groundwork for another White House campaign, including meeting major donors, hiring political staff and travelling to battleground states to campaign for Democratic candidates ahead of the November midterm elections. Harris, the daughter of an Indian mother and Jamaican father, has publicly maintained that she has not decided whether to make another attempt to become America's first woman president. "I have not decided if I’m going to run again," Harris said at an NAACP event in Michigan last month, according to the newspaper. "I do sincerely believe ’28 won’t matter if we don’t get through ’26," she added, emphasising the importance of the upcoming congressional elections. A spokesman for Harris declined to comment on the Journal's report. Harris was the Democratic presidential nominee in 2024 and lost to Republican Donald Trump. According to the newspaper, some Democratic donors have privately questioned whether Harris should seek the nomination again, while several party figures believe Democrats should consider a fresh candidate in 2028. The report said Emhoff's concerns come after years of supporting Harris through demanding political campaigns and intense public scrutiny. In her memoir, "107 Days," Harris described the personal toll of the 2024 campaign on their marriage, including the pressure created by political attacks and public criticism. Since leaving Washington, Emhoff has resumed practising law in Los Angeles, while the couple have purchased a home in Malibu. Despite uncertainty surrounding her presidential ambitions, Harris has remained politically active. The Journal reported that she has participated in several private fundraisers in California, including events supporting Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate David Crowley and Nevada gubernatorial candidate Aaron Ford. She also joined a Democratic National Committee mobilisation call involving more than 2,000 volunteers, encouraging campaign workers to reach voters in competitive states. Harris is expected to campaign in Nevada and Georgia, including on behalf of Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff, who is seeking re-election. She has also strengthened her political operation, working with advisers including former ambassador Candace Bond and communications director Eduardo Negrón. The report said Harris has maintained ties with Democratic strategist Brian Fallon, who worked on her 2024 presidential campaign. Her political activities come as several prominent Democrats weigh potential presidential bids. California Governor Gavin Newsom, another possible contender, has said he would not run if Harris entered the race, according to the newspaper. Harris continues to have support among important Democratic constituencies, particularly Black women, and has been campaigning to mobilise voters in competitive states. Democratic strategist Donna Brazile, who remains in contact with Harris, told the Journal that the former vice president was concentrating on helping Democratic candidates in the November elections. Harris served as vice president from 2021 to 2025 under Biden, becoming the first woman, first Black American and first person of South Asian descent to hold the office. Before that, she represented California in the US Senate and served as the state's attorney general.

news.text: The US-India Strategic Partnership Forum (USISPF) has defended the economic contribution of employment-based immigration programmes in the United States, warning against overlooking the role of skilled foreign professionals as the Trump administration intensifies scrutiny of green card sponsorship by major technology companies.In a statement issued on Friday, USISPF described the Green Card and H-1B programmes as among the United States' most significant economic policy success stories, arguing that they have helped drive innovation, create jobs and strengthen the country's global competitiveness.The intervention comes after the US administration announced the suspension of eight major technology companies from the Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, a key step in the employer-sponsored green card process. The affected firms include Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. The administration has cited alleged fraud and misuse of immigration pathways in taking action against the companies."The Green Card and H-1B programs are among the United States' most significant economic policy success stories," USISPF said, highlighting their contribution to American growth, technological advancement and business development.USISPF Highlights Economic ContributionCiting an analysis of 2022 US Census Bureau data, the forum said the legal immigration pathways had generated $2.1 trillion in combined household income, contributed $382.9 billion in federal taxes and $196.3 billion in state and local taxes, while leaving $1.6 trillion in spending power.The statement also pointed to the achievements of immigrant innovators recognised at a White House ceremony where President Donald Trump presented the National Medals of Science and the National Medals of Technology and Innovation to leading scientists and technologists.Five of the six recipients, according to USISPF, were born outside the United States. The forum cited their achievements as evidence of the contribution of immigrant talent to American innovation and prosperity.The organisation said it supported the administration's efforts to prevent fraud and abuse in immigration programmes, particularly following the US Department of Labor's recent action concerning PERM."We fully support the administration's efforts to prevent fraud and abuse in legal immigration programs," the statement said, adding that such practices could undermine the domestic job market and that the programmes must operate with integrity and in accordance with their intended purpose.However, USISPF stressed that efforts to enforce immigration rules should also recognise the wider economic benefits of legal migration.Indian Americans At The Centre Of DebateThe forum singled out the Indian American community as an example of how skilled immigration can benefit the United States over generations.Although Indian Americans account for approximately 1.5% of the US population, they contribute around 6% of the country's gross domestic product, the statement said. It also highlighted their educational achievements, business participation and role in the technology sector.USISPF said Indian Americans had co-founded 72 of the 648 unicorn companies in the United States in 2024, underlining their contribution to entrepreneurship and technological development."Generations of Indian Americans have come to this country through legal immigration pathways, worked hard, pursued education, built businesses, and become successful, tax-paying members of American society," the statement said.The forum argued that these contributions extend beyond individual success, strengthening economic ties and shared values between India and the United States.Balancing Enforcement With Talent NeedsThe PERM suspension has raised concerns over the future of employment-based permanent residency for eligible foreign professionals working at the affected companies. The measure targets the green card certification process rather than automatically cancelling existing H-1B visas, although it could disrupt some employees' pathways to permanent residency.USISPF said it shared the administration's objective of maintaining America's position as a global technology leader while protecting employment opportunities for domestic workers."We share the administration's goal of helping the United States succeed as a global technology leader by attracting the best global technology talent while sustaining a strong domestic job market," it said.The statement reflects the challenge facing US policymakers: addressing alleged immigration abuses without weakening the country's ability to attract skilled professionals. For Indian technology workers and businesses with operations in the US, the outcome of the evolving debate could have significant implications for recruitment, workforce mobility and long-term residency prospects.

news.title: UN condemns US plan to livestream Fort Hood gunman’s execution
news.text:
US President Donald Trump's administration is facing international criticism over plans to livestream the firing squad execution of Nidal Hasan, a former US Army psychiatrist convicted of killing 13 people in 2009.

The Pentagon confirmed Thursday that Hasan, 56, would be executed on December 3 at Fort Hood, Texas.

The United Nations human rights office warned that broadcasting the execution would “breach the absolute prohibition of torture”.

Former US Secretary of State Hillary Clinton condemned the decision, writing: “A barbaric idea, beneath our dignity as a country. Push back on this.”

British equalities minister Bridget Phillipson also described the proposal as “rather disturbing”.

US President Donald Trump approved the execution method following a recommendation from Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.

Vice-President JD Vance said he would not watch the broadcast but defended the focus on Hasan’s crimes.

“Whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope the people don’t forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people,” Vance said.

Hasan was convicted in 2013 of 13 murders and 32 attempted murders following the Fort Hood shooting. He was partly paralysed during his arrest and now uses a wheelchair.

The execution would be the first carried out by a US military firing squad since 1945.

news.title: US judge rules DOJ using state voter rolls unconstitutional
news.text:
A ​US judge ruled on Friday that the Justice Department’s push to obtain state voter rolls and check them ‌against a federal immigration database to demand that states remove voters it deemed ineligible was unlawful.

US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan’s decision marked the latest setback for President Donald Trump’s push to expand federal control over election administration ahead of the November 3 midterms, with his Republican Party battling to hold majorities ​in both houses of Congress.

In a 78-page decision siding with a challenge to the Justice Department’s practice brought by ​watchdog group Common Cause, Sooknanan wrote that the Justice Department had downplayed the risk that its practice ⁠would wrongfully disenfranchise eligible US citizens despite evidence that the immigration database, known as SAVE, could be inaccurate.

“The challenged policy ​represents the federal government’s attempt to decide who gets to vote. But Congress has left that authority where our Constitution has always ​placed it: with the states,” wrote Sooknanan, who is based in Washington and was appointed by Democratic President Joe Biden.

Supreme Court Paused Previous Ruling 

Ming Cheung, a lawyer with the American Civil Liberties Union who represented the plaintiffs, said in a statement, “Today’s ruling makes clear that the administration cannot ​use the federal government to disrupt elections.”

The Justice Department is reviewing the decision, a spokesperson said.

In a separate case, Sooknanan blocked the ​Trump administration in June from using an expanded version of the SAVE database to check the accuracy of voter rolls. The US Supreme ‌Court temporarily paused ⁠that decision last month.

Federal election law prohibits the systematic review of voter rolls in the 90 days before any federal election, potentially blunting the impact of both Sooknanan’s decision and the Supreme Court’s pause of her previous order on the upcoming midterms.

Latest Defeat for Justice Department

Trump, who falsely claims his loss in the 2020 presidential election was due to voter fraud, ordered the Justice Department ​last year to crack down ​on voting by ineligible people, ⁠despite multiple state audits and independent studies showing such voter fraud is rare.

The Justice Department then demanded that nearly all 50 states hand over their complete, unredacted voter rolls, including sensitive information ​such as voters’ Social Security numbers or dates of birth.

Eighteen mostly Republican-led states complied. After ​receiving the voter ⁠data, the Justice Department ran it through SAVE and alerted states to voters found to be non-citizens so the states could remove them.

Sooknanan said the Trump administration’s expansion of SAVE meant it now contained citizenship data from the Social Security Administration, which could be outdated, ⁠meaning many ​immigrants who had since been naturalized as US citizens would still be flagged ​as non-citizens.

The Justice Department sued 30 Democratic-led and Republican states that refused to hand over their unredacted voter rolls, as well as Washington, DC. It has lost ​26 of those cases so far, without winning one.
news.summary: US District Judge Sparkle Sooknanan ruled that the Justice Department's push to obtain state voter rolls to check citizenship status is unconstitutional.

 US announces sanctions on ICC, hours after Nobel award to former judge 







WASHINGTON, United States (AFP) — The United States (US) on Friday announced sanctions on the International Criminal Court, vowing to cripple the tribunal’s operations just hours after the Nobel Peace Prize went to a former ICC judge who warned of mounting political attacks on the court.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington would ban transactions with what he called a “rogue court,” escalating a long-running campaign by President Donald Trump’s administration against the Hague-based tribunal.

“Either the ICC will end its threats, or we will end the ICC,” Rubio said in a statement.

But the immediate impact of the sanctions was softened by a series of exemptions that offer a de facto six-month grace period.

The State Department said that was meant to give the court’s member states time to show “meaningful progress” toward addressing US concerns.

The grace period could be adjusted depending on the “success or failure” of those efforts, the department added.

The court rejected the US sanctions as an attack on international law and warned in a statement that “history will judge this moment.”

Countries including Canada, France, Germany, Japan and the United Kingdom said in a joint statement that they “strongly disagree” with the announcement.

UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the US decision “a serious blow to our collective pursuit of international criminal justice, of which the ICC is a key pillar.”

The European Union called the sanctions “deeply regrettable” and said it was “ready to take any necessary measures to enable the court to carry out its work.”

The European Commission, the EU’s executive arm, said it hoped the six-month delay meant “there is room for dialogue.”

Rights group Amnesty International urged countries to “resist” the move, saying the sanctions were “designed to isolate and ultimately destroy” the court.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, who faces an ICC arrest warrant over alleged crimes in Gaza, praised the US action.

“The ICC is not a court. It is a political body that poses a mortal threat to law-abiding democracies worldwide and to the very idea of national sovereignty,” his office posted on X.

The move came on the same day the Norwegian Nobel Committee awarded the peace prize to South Africa’s Navi Pillay, an 85-year-old jurist who headed the Rwanda genocide tribunal, served on the ICC and later led a UN commission that accused Israel of genocide in Gaza.

Rubio’s statement did not mention Pillay or the Nobel award.

He said the sanctions were needed to protect security personnel and elected officials from prosecution by a court the United States has never joined.

“President Trump will never allow the International Criminal Court to prosecute Americans,” Rubio said, adding that the measures would cut off the court’s resources and cripple “its ability to operate.”

The top US diplomat said Washington had for more than a year spelled out “basic gestures of good faith” it expected from the court, and had held off on the designation in hopes that the ICC or its member states would change course.

He said no “meaningful steps” had been taken to address US concerns.

Rubio also called on US allies that belong to the court and “rely on American service members for their defense” to rein it in, warning that otherwise Washington would keep working to dismantle the ICC “brick by brick.”

The Trump administration had already sanctioned 17 people linked to the court, including its prosecutor and several judges, over the ICC’s investigations involving the United States and Israel, which is also not a member.

Trump last month called on all ICC member states to quit the body, denouncing it as “out of control” and a “rogue institution.”

news.title: Democrats accuse Trump of betraying Ukraine, allies in diesel deal with Putin
news.text:
WASHINGTON: Top Democrats accused President Donald Trump of betraying Ukraine, European allies and US national security after he announced a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to obtain diesel, while Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky condemned the move as a weak decision that could prolong Russia’s war against his country.

Zelensky said the agreement would benefit Moscow by enabling it to continue its military campaign, warning that Russia would repay the United States with “further terror and perfidy.”

“I believe our team is simply being used as a smokescreen. And that is certainly not fair. It is certainly not how partners should treat each other,” Zelensky said in remarks released by the Ukrainian Embassy in Washington.

His reaction came as Trump’s envoy Steve Witkoff and son-in-law Jared Kushner met Ukrainian officials in Miami to discuss a proposal to end the war.

Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren, the ranking Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, denounced Trump’s announcement as a betrayal of Ukraine, European allies and US national security.

“Enough is enough,” the senators said in a statement. “The President must end his war with Iran instead of funding Russia’s war machine.”

Sharp reversal

Trump announced the agreement on social media on Friday following a phone call with Putin, in which the two leaders were expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump said Moscow would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by another 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons “immediately thereafter.” Russia would deliver an additional 3 million tons “within a short period of time,” he said.

The announcement marked a sharp reversal of years of US pressure on Moscow over its invasion of Ukraine and came just weeks before the US midterm elections, as rising energy costs put pressure on American consumers.

It also appeared to contradict a sweeping Russia sanctions law Trump signed last month, which seeks to restrict Moscow’s oil and gas revenues and directs the administration to target countries that continue purchasing Russian energy.

Democratic Sen. Richard Blumenthal, a co-sponsor of the sanctions legislation, said the decision made the United States complicit in Russia’s war.

“This agreement with a murdering dictator is a stain on our nation’s character, an insult to Lindsey Graham’s memory, and directly contrary to Congress’s intent in our bipartisan sanctions bill,” Blumenthal said.

Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called the announcement “infuriating.”

“This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn’t the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia,” Beyer said in a statement on X.

Sanctions policy in question

The agreement has raised questions about whether the White House will enforce the new sanctions law as Congress intended. The legislation provides for sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers, bans new US investment in Russia and restricts dealings in Russian sovereign debt.

It also directs Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100 percent on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15 percent of Russia’s natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.

The United States has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned the purchases following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine, according to the US Energy Information Administration.

Shortly after Trump’s announcement, the Treasury Department issued a temporary license allowing Russian diesel shipments loaded onto tankers as of Friday to be delivered without facing US sanctions until April 2027.

The six-month relief is the latest in a series of US measures easing restrictions on Russian fuel shipments since the war in Iran began earlier this year. It is, however, the first time since Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 that Washington has relaxed diesel sanctions for longer than the standard 30-day period.

The extensions underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has strengthened Moscow’s ability to profit from energy exports, even as Washington continues to publicly support Ukraine.

Impact on fuel prices uncertain

Trump defended the agreement as a way to lower domestic fuel costs, saying on social media that reducing prices for Americans, particularly farmers, ranchers and truckers, was his top priority.

Global fuel prices have surged as the war in Iran has disrupted energy markets. Although diesel futures prices fell following the announcement on Friday, the US national average remained high at $6.28 a gallon, according to AAA, after reaching a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.

Leaving the White House for a campaign rally later Friday, Trump thanked Putin for the deal.

“We have massive amounts of oil coming into our country, and it’s diesel, which is what we want. So, thank you,” Trump said. He did not respond to shouted questions about Zelensky’s criticism.

The White House did not immediately answer questions about who would pay for the Russian diesel or when the supplies would become available.

In a statement released by the Kremlin, Putin said the two leaders had devoted “significant attention to the prospects of resolving the Ukrainian crisis” and discussed the situation surrounding Iran and other aspects of bilateral relations.

Russia had “confirmed its readiness to supply oil and oil products to the American and global markets,” Putin said, adding that he was confident the move would benefit the global economy.

Russian presidential aide Yuri Ushakov declined to say whether Washington had offered concessions in exchange for the supplies or what, if anything, Moscow had been promised.

Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said Moscow was immediately beginning to lift diesel export restrictions ahead of schedule and could start supplying the United States this month. He added that Russia’s domestic market would remain fully supplied.

Russia, once a major diesel exporter, had restricted exports since July as Ukrainian attacks on its oil refineries and strong domestic demand strained supplies. The International Energy Agency estimates that Russian diesel output has fallen by about 30 percent.

Energy analysts cautioned that the agreement might do little to reduce prices because additional Russian supplies could simply redirect fuel from existing customers rather than increase the amount available globally.

Clayton Seigle, an energy strategist at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, said the deal was unlikely to have a significant effect on prices but would greatly benefit Russia and Putin, who are seeking to offload summer-grade diesel before switching to heavier winter and Arctic grades.

Michael Lynch of the Energy Policy Research Foundation, a nonpartisan research institution focused on energy and economics, said diverting Russian diesel to the United States would force existing customers to seek supplies elsewhere, potentially keeping prices largely unchanged.

Zelensky, meanwhile, warned that the arrangement would allow Russia to kill more people, prolong the war and inflict greater damage.

“It plays into Russia’s hands — allowing it to kill more, wage war for longer, have even less respect for America, and inflict even greater losses and damage on the world,” he said.

news.title: Moment stunned Donald Trump discovers legendary Chicago Bears coach Mike Ditka has died as President pays tribute to his 'big supporter'
news.text:
Cameras captured the moment where President Donald Trump was informed of the passing of Chicago Bears player and coach Mike Ditka.

Ditka, a Hall of Fame player and coach who led the Bears to their only Super Bowl title, passed away on Friday at the age of 86.

On the lawn of the White House, joined by boxing legend Mike Tyson and New York Yankees president Randy Levine, Trump was asked about Ditka's passing - only to reveal he hadn't heard the news.

'Oh, he did?' Trump asked before turning to his two companions and saying, 'Mike Ditka.'

Trump continued: 'He was a great guy. He was with me all the way. He was tough.'

Then, in an echo of his reaction to the death of former Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsberg, Trump said, 'Mike Ditka is... that's a sad one, you're just telling me that now for the first time.'

Trump closed: 'He was great. He was great. He was a... He was a big supporter of mine. Won the Super Bowl in '86. Yeah, no, he was a winner. He was a tough cookie. He was great.'

The President was speaking just before he left the White House with Tyson for a rally in Syracuse, New York on Friday evening.

After playing just a few seasons for the Bears, Ditka returned to Chicago as a head coach in 1982 and helped lead the team to their most successful era ever.

He became a popular figure in the city and in sports culture, leveraging this into a broadcasting career at ESPN. 

Ditka's high-profile status also made him an effective advocate to secure improved health and retirement benefits for former players.

His name also circulated for years in Illinois political circles. Though he never ran for office, Ditka described himself as a staunch conservative and was mentioned several times as a possible Republican candidate, including a congressional race against then state Rep. Barack Obama for the US Senate.

In his later years, Ditka was a staunch supporter of Trump's - saying in 2016: 'I support Trump all the way. I really do.'

news.title: 14th review – Ava DuVernay’s galvanizing documentary is a remarkable achievement
news.text:
Carla Hayden with Ava DuVernay on 14th. Photograph: Paul Garnes/NetflixView image in fullscreenCarla Hayden with Ava DuVernay on 14th. Photograph: Paul Garnes/NetflixReview14th review – Ava DuVernay’s galvanizing documentary is a remarkable achievementNew York film festival: the director has made a fascinating and troubling companion piece to her Netflix documentary 13th, which takes a fiery look at American injustice

It feels at once like the blink of an eye and an eternity since Ava DuVernay’s documentary 13th arrived on Netflix, a month before the election of Donald Trump to his first term as president. The intervening decade has more or less borne out the film’s thesis on the enduring specter of white supremacy in American life: that a clause within the 13th amendment abolishing chattel slavery – that involuntary servitude could be used as punishment for a crime – was immediately and continually exploited to criminalize black people, mass incarceration thus being the modern incarnation of America’s original sin.

Read moreThe Oscar-nominated film, which saw a surge in viewership during the protests of 2020, has remained both a time capsule of late Obama-era moral clarity and, arguably, the acclaimed director’s best picture. At least, until now – 14th, DuVernay’s sequel, of sorts, soon also to arrive on Netflix, is just as lucid and galvanizing as its predecessor, with an updated, more pressing urgency befitting a democracy in distress.

The new film focuses its brisk 110 minutes on the 14th amendment, adopted in the aftermath of the civil war, in a moment of profound political destabilization. The five-point statute may be lesser-known and not widely understood, but the film summarily makes the case for its status as the “workhorse amendment”, the “magnum opus of American democracy”, to quote several of the film’s illustrious figures. Once again, DuVernay marshals a murderers’ row of constitutional experts and political figures, from Stacey Abrams to Hasan Piker, Equal Justice Initiative founder Bryan Stevenson to Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (and also, for some token Republican context, the former “Never Trumper” senator Jeff Flake and current anti-birthright citizenship Florida congresswoman Anna Paulina Luna, who gets ruthlessly factchecked by some title cards). DuVernay stages her largely persuasive cast – lawyers, politicians, civil rights organizers and more – in striking, stately tableaux, before marble and monuments, underscoring the argument for the amendment’s status as the epitome of humanist sophistication: government by the people, for all the people.

View image in fullscreenAva DuVernay with Dr David Blight. Photograph: Courtesy of NetflixThe heavy lifting in this argument is cogently provided by Sherrilyn Ifill, the former president of the NAACP Legal Defense Fund and a law professor at Howard University, where she founded the 14th Amendment Center for Law and Democracy; Ifill is a warm yet precise narrator, masterfully laying out the case that the verbose, multi-pronged amendment is actually the scaffolding upon which hang our hopes for a true multi-racial, multi-faith democracy. It is the 14th amendment that guarantees birthright citizenship as well as voting rights, that bars insurrectionists from again holding public office (you know what awful, infuriating footage is coming, though it is necessary) and, through numerous legal defenses, allowed interracial couples to marry and women to obtain credit cards.

To summarily stamp down its importance and radical historical context, DuVernay employs many of the same techniques as 13th to arguably greater effect: trenchant illustrations, blistering through the Trump years as a literal desecration of the 14th amendment’s five-pointed star; needle-drops from Kendrick Lamar to Fleetwood Mac to James Brown. And, most potently, adding dimension and movement to archival photographs of both the Black flourishing in the immediate aftermath of the civil war – formerly enslaved people in the halls of Congress, churches, universities and other institutions – as well as the swift backlash to Reconstruction in the form of terroristic vigilante violence, penal colonies and Jim Crow segregation.

It’s a bracing, riveting torrent dense with facts and figures – the 4,400 known lynchings of Black Americans between the civil war and the second world war, the 2,629 monuments to the Confederate slave republic erected in the same period, the galling visual evidence of it all – as well as some jittery timeline hopping. Some tangents, such as time with Devon Henry, the Black contractor tasked with dismantling several Confederate monuments in Virginia, are admirable but a bit afield, threatening to dilute the film’s tight, punchy focus on the amendment’s oft-challenged fortitude.

Still, it paints a damning portrait of the Trump administration and the larger Maga movement, with its explicit invocation of a different, better past, as a continuation of the “Lost Cause” mythology of the Confederacy – a false narrative of historical memory that constitutes, to quote the southern historian Karen Cox, the “most successful propaganda campaign in the history of the United States”.

The film’s final section, on the Trump administration’s all-out assault on every article of the amendment, is nothing any follower of US news doesn’t already know, but still burns with righteous anger and alarm. What was the insurrection clause if not an attempt to prevent, and then punish, the January 6 rioters who Trump wanted US taxpayers to compensate? What are masked ICE arrests and killings, played in one extremely effective if difficult montage, if not a direct violation of due process?

Quibbles aside, 14th is a rare feat, at once informative, infuriating and undeniable. That DuVernay may too often repeat the same clip or phrase is largely outweighed by the import of the statement, such as one written by Frederick Douglass and delivered by Ifill: the spirit of white supremacy will not die out in a year; it will not die out in an age. As 14th illustrates, that legacy is the one we’ve all inherited, and it is ignored or underestimated at our peril.

14th is premiering at the New York film festival and will be released in cinemas on 27 November and available on Netflix on 4 December

news.title: Katie Zacharia: 'Honor of a Lifetime' to Serve as White House Press Secretary
news.text:
Newly named White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Friday that being selected to serve in the role is “the honor of a lifetime.”

Zacharia took to X and Truth Social to thank President Donald Trump for the opportunity after he officially announced her appointment earlier in the afternoon.

“Serving President Trump and the American people at this critical 250-year mark is the honor of a lifetime,” she wrote.

“President Trump has shown America that we can be great again, and he works to effectuate that greatness every single day. His confidence is a true privilege, and his leadership is a blessing to this country,” she added.

Zacharia looks forward to working with reporters in the White House and around the nation to share the Trump administration’s record.

“The work ahead is to continue delivering strong results for our Country and communicating to the American people the major wins that this Administration is making every single day,” she wrote.

“I look forward to working with the White House press corps, and with reporters across the country, to get that record out,” she added.

She also gave a nod to her predecessor Karoline Leavitt, who left the administration at the end of August to spend more time with her young children.

“Following the fabulous Karoline Leavitt is a high standard, and one worth meeting,” she said. “God bless President Trump, and God bless America.”

Zacharia, who earned a Juris Doctor from Pepperdine University, is leaving her role as senior communications adviser at Truth Social and Trump Media & Technology Group to serve as the 37th press secretary. Before joining Truth Social in June, she worked as deputy assistant secretary to public affairs and a spokeswoman at the Department of Homeland Security.

Trump called Zacharia “a great person” while departing the White House alongside Mike Tyson, en route to New York, Friday afternoon.

“She’s a friend of most of you. I know she likes people. She likes all of you, actually. I don’t know if that’s good or bad … she’s going to be, I think, terrific,” he told reporters.
news.summary:
Newly named White House press secretary Katie Zacharia said Friday that being selected to serve in the role is "the honor of a lifetime."
